value-reference-types.title: Value types and reference types
value-reference-types.short: Whether an assignment carries the value itself or a reference to an object.
value-reference-types.summary: C# types are broadly divided into value types and reference types, and assignment and mutation behave differently for each.
value-reference-types.why: int is a value type, so its value is copied. List<T> is a reference type, so the reference to the same object is copied.
value-reference-types.tips: Even for a reference type, the reference itself is passed as a value. Passing by reference with ref is a separate mechanism.

boxing-unboxing.title: Boxing and unboxing
boxing-unboxing.short: Conversions that occur when a value type is treated as object or an interface type.
boxing-unboxing.summary: Converting a value type to object or an interface type can wrap the value in an object representation.
boxing-unboxing.why: Value types and reference types use different storage models, so boxing creates an object that can hold the value through a reference.
boxing-unboxing.tips: Generic APIs usually avoid unnecessary boxing more easily than older non-generic APIs.

var-keyword.title: var and type inference
var-keyword.short: Let the compiler determine a local variable's type from its initializer.
var-keyword.summary: var is not dynamic typing. The compiler determines a specific static type from the initialization expression.
var-keyword.why: Because the type is fixed at compile time, the variable cannot later hold an unrelated type.
var-keyword.tips: var is convenient when the type is obvious from the right-hand side; use an explicit type when it makes code easier to understand.

const-readonly.title: const and readonly
const-readonly.short: Two ways to represent values that should not change.
const-readonly.summary: const represents compile-time constants, while readonly is commonly used for fields that are assigned during construction and not changed afterward.
const-readonly.why: A runtime value such as DateTime.Now cannot be const, but it can be assigned to a readonly field.
const-readonly.tips: A public const value is embedded into consuming assemblies, so library compatibility matters when changing it.

properties.title: Properties
properties.short: Members that look like fields while allowing controlled read and write behavior.
properties.summary: Properties expose values through get and set accessors and can include validation or computed behavior when needed.
properties.why: Compared with a public field, a property makes read/write permissions and later behavior changes easier to express.
properties.tips: Use init when a value should only be assignable during initialization.

records.title: record
records.short: Define data-focused types concisely with value-based equality.
records.summary: record is useful for data-centric types and provides value-based equality so instances with the same components can compare as equal.
records.why: Unlike the default reference identity of a normal class, record generates equality based on its data components.
records.tips: A with expression can create a new value while changing only selected members.

interfaces.title: interface
interfaces.short: Describe a contract for capabilities a type provides.
interfaces.summary: An interface expresses what a type can do rather than how it does it, allowing multiple implementations to be used through the same abstraction.
interfaces.why: Callers can depend on only the capabilities they need instead of depending on a specific class.
interfaces.tips: .NET uses interfaces extensively, including IEnumerable<T> and IDisposable.

generics.title: Generics
generics.short: Accept types as parameters to write reusable, type-safe code.
generics.summary: Generics let code specify a concrete type at use time, as with T in List<T>.
generics.why: The same logic can work with int, string, and other types without duplication while preserving type information.
generics.tips: Use where T : ... constraints to restrict which types are valid.

delegates.title: delegate
delegates.short: A type for storing and passing methods as values.
delegates.summary: A delegate can refer to methods with a specific parameter list and return type and can be handled much like a value.
delegates.why: Passing behavior as an argument lets callers supply operations such as sorting rules or transformations.
delegates.tips: Action is a common delegate type with no return value; Func represents delegates that return a value.

events.title: event
events.summary: Based on delegates, an event exposes subscription and unsubscription while restricting who can raise the notification.
events.why: This separates the object that publishes a notification from the code that reacts to it.
events.tips: Leaving a subscription attached to a long-lived publisher can keep references alive longer than intended.

lambda.title: Lambda expressions
lambda.short: Write small pieces of behavior without naming a method.
lambda.summary: Syntax such as x => x * 2 concisely defines behavior that can be converted to a delegate.
lambda.why: LINQ and callback APIs often need short operations that are convenient to provide inline.
lambda.tips: For multiple statements, use the block form x => { ... }.

linq-deferred.title: LINQ deferred execution
linq-deferred.short: Many operators such as Where do not enumerate immediately.
linq-deferred.summary: Many LINQ operations returning IEnumerable<T> do their actual work only when the sequence is enumerated, for example by foreach.
linq-deferred.why: Calling Where does not freeze the result; the source numbers are read when enumeration happens.
linq-deferred.tips: Use ToList or ToArray when you need to materialize and freeze the result at that point.

ienumerable.title: IEnumerable<T>
ienumerable.short: An interface representing a sequence whose elements can be enumerated in order.
ienumerable.summary: IEnumerable<T> is the basis of foreach and much of LINQ and represents a sequence that can provide elements one at a time.
ienumerable.why: Code can depend only on the ability to enumerate rather than on a concrete collection such as List<T>.
ienumerable.tips: IEnumerable<T> alone does not guarantee cheap Count access or indexing.

async-await.title: async / await
async-await.short: Wait for long-running operations without simply blocking the current thread.
async-await.summary: Awaiting an asynchronous operation that returns Task lets the method continue from that point after the operation completes.
async-await.why: The method is structured as a continuation that resumes later instead of simply stopping the current thread for the whole wait.
async-await.tips: async does not automatically mean the method runs on another thread.

task.title: Task
task.short: Represent an operation that will complete in the future and its state.
task.summary: Task represents asynchronous completion, failure, or cancellation and can be awaited.
task.why: Even when a result does not exist yet, Task<T> can represent the value that will become available when the operation finishes.
task.tips: Task.Run is useful for moving CPU-bound work to the thread pool; it is not required for every asynchronous operation.

idisposable.title: IDisposable and using
idisposable.short: Reliably release resources when they are no longer needed.
idisposable.summary: Objects such as files and streams may implement IDisposable when they require explicit cleanup.
idisposable.why: The garbage collector alone cannot guarantee that operating-system resources such as file handles are released at the exact time you need.
idisposable.tips: A using statement and a using directive share the same keyword but serve different purposes.

equality.title: == and Equals
equality.short: Ways to determine whether two values are equal.
equality.summary: The meaning of == depends on the type: some types compare values, while others may compare references.
equality.why: string defines == as content comparison. For user-defined types, equality behavior depends on the implementation.
equality.tips: Use ReferenceEquals when you specifically need to know whether two references point to the same object.

pattern-matching.title: Pattern matching
pattern-matching.short: Use patterns such as is to test a value's type or shape and capture values safely.
pattern-matching.summary: Pattern matching lets you combine a type test with extracting a strongly typed variable in one expression.
pattern-matching.why: After value is string text succeeds, the compiler knows that text is a string inside that branch.
pattern-matching.tips: This is safer than directly casting an uncertain object. See [[invalid-cast|InvalidCastException]] for casts that fail at runtime.
